answer:
HYPOTHESIS: Between 1990 and 1996, wealth inequality increased within both white males and white females in the NLSY79 cohort, and the increase took the form of polarization rather than a uniform spreading of the distribution. In both groups, mean composite wealth rose (white males: $88,163 → $131,792; white females: $99,605 → $128,837, nominal) while the median fell sharply (males: $15,601 → $8,900; females: $20,100 → $8,825) and the share of respondents with exactly zero wealth grew from roughly 26% to roughly 43% in each group. The upper tail pulled away from the middle: the P90/P50 ratio nearly tripled (males 13.8 → 37.5; females 12.1 → 37.6) and the overall Gini rose modestly (males 0.781 → 0.794; females 0.763 → 0.778), while the top-decile wealth share stayed essentially flat (males ~0.62; females ~0.59). We therefore hypothesize that 1990–1996 wealth growth among whites accrued disproportionately to those already at the top, hollowing out the middle and accumulating a larger zero-wealth mass, so that top-versus-middle inequality rose for both sexes. This increase is robust on top-vs-middle measures — it survives removal of the single extreme 1990 outlier (−$866,400) and top-1% winsorization (Gini still rises: males 0.763 → 0.784; females 0.733 → 0.769). It is, however, sensitive to how zero and negative wealth are treated: on a positive-holders-only Gini the direction reverses (males 0.689 → 0.623; females 0.681 → 0.599), meaning dispersion among positive-wealth holders actually narrowed while the zero-wealth mass grew; the polarization claim, not a universal "Gini rose" claim, is the defensible one. Side-by-side levels: white females had the higher median in 1990 ($20,100 vs $15,601), but by 1996 the two groups' medians had converged to ~$8,800–8,900, with females' Gini remaining slightly lower than males' in both years. Incarceration (ever_jailed, descriptive only, small n: 57 jailed white males, 12 jailed white females) is associated with much lower wealth (jailed white males' median fell to $0 by 1996), but with n this small and a jailing window (1985–1994) overlapping the wealth window, this is a caveat, not part of the primary claim. Limitations: values are assumed to be nominal US dollars with no deflator available in the data, so no inflation adjustment was possible; the exact construction of the five-item composite wealth variable cannot be verified from the file alone; and P10 = $0 in both waves makes P50/P10 undefined.

WORKFLOW: (1) Inspected data/nls_incarceration_processed.csv: 12,013 rows × 6 columns, no missing values; race×sex counts white male 3,469 / white female 3,630; identified 614 negative and 2,975 zero wealth values in 1990 and 358 negative and 4,561 zeros in 1996, plus a single 1990 outlier of −866,400. (2) Executed outputs/analysis_wealth_inequality.py (pandas/numpy): computed per group-year mean, median, SD, CV, P90/P50, P50/P10, top-decile share, and Gini via the mean-absolute-difference formula valid with zeros/negatives, on white males and white females with negatives and zeros retained. (3) Sensitivity analyses: (A) removed the 1990 minimum outlier; (B) winsorized the top 1% per group-year; (C) recomputed Gini on positive wealth only. (4) Produced a descriptive ever_jailed breakdown with an explicit small-n and non-causal caveat. (5) Wrote results to outputs/primary_stats_white_1990_1996.csv, outputs/sensitivity_outlier_removed.csv, outputs/sensitivity_winsorized.csv, outputs/ever_jailed_descriptive.csv. Two implementation bugs found and fixed during execution (outlier row initially not dropped; sensitivity table initially built from the original frame) — the final run is the verified one. No new computation after researcher approval of this synthesis.
